narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 64.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile in both years—one compared to an average of around 6 among accepted students—signals consistently lower academic performance relative to your peers, which the model sees as a major risk for bar exam success.

Next, your family income bracket worked mildly in your favor. Being in the middle-income group is fairly common among accepted students, and the model slightly reduced its estimate of failure risk based on this.

Your LSAT score of 22.7, well below the 37.2 average of accepted applicants, was the third most important factor and pushed the prediction back toward failure. Combined with your undergraduate GPA of 2.5 versus the 3.23 average among those admitted, these academic indicators reinforced the model’s concern.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record. Retaking the LSAT, enrolling in a strong academic support program, or gaining additional legal experience could improve your profile for future applications. Consider reapplying once you can demonstrate clearer evidence of readiness for the demands of law school and the bar exam.
